title: Starting up a project: practices applied and judging the process
blurb: Say which practice each starting up action applies, and judge whether starting up is being done in a proportionate, effective way.
question: Before initiation, a board member asks for a full investment appraisal with detailed costs for every stage. Is this an appropriate way to carry out starting up a project, and why?

teach.body: Formally: each process applies the practices in set ways (tab 13.3), and the Practitioner exam asks you to analyse whether a process is effective and fit for purpose against its purpose, objectives, tailoring and roles (13.1 to 13.7). In plain English: name the practice behind an action, then ask whether the action helps answer 'do we have a viable and worthwhile project?' without doing more than needed.

head: Practice
What starting up does
Where it lands
rows: Sets up the daily log; gathers lessons
Defines the project approach; develops the PPD
Identifies an initial set of key risks
Appoints the executive, PM and team
teach.caption: The first four rows are the official tab 13.3 extracts the exam uses most. Business case and organizing follow from the products each activity creates.

teach.body: Starting up exists to check the prerequisites for initiation: is there a viable and worthwhile project? It is as much about stopping poorly conceived ideas as approving good ones, so it is a lighter process than initiation and does the minimum necessary. The decision to start must be explicit, and no time should be wasted initiating on unsound assumptions about scope, timescales, acceptance criteria or constraints.

rows.label: Business case
values: Full, with plan costs and risks

teach.h: How much starting up is right?

bands.label: Too light: no lessons, no PPD
Too heavy: initiation work done early

teach.caption: Both ends fail the purpose. Skipping lessons repeats old mistakes; a full business case or detailed design before authority wastes effort on an idea that may be stopped.

items: Purpose: does the action help decide whether initiation is worthwhile?
Proportion: is it the minimum needed, or initiation or delivery work done too early?
Roles: is the right role doing it (appointments by the executive, PM preparing the products)?
Practices: is each practice applied as recommended (for example initial risks noted in the daily log)?
Tailoring: does the way it is done fit the project's size, risk and context?

teach.h: Is this starting up action effective?

root.label: Does it help decide if initiation is worthwhile?

children.label: Out of place: delivery or detail too early
Is the right role doing it?

teach.body: Andrew Mallory, executive, appoints Kezia Oduya as project manager. Kezia opens a daily log and a lessons log and asks the council's senior auditor, who reviewed two earlier events, what went wrong. She notes in the daily log the risk that the safety advisory group may not approve the safety plan in time. She records quality expectations such as a certified course. A cabinet member wants a detailed marketing plan now; Kezia keeps starting up light and leaves that work for later stages.

teach.text: Classic traps: initial risks found in starting up go in the daily log, NOT in the risk management approach (which holds procedures, never specific risks) and not in a risk register that does not exist yet. A full business case in starting up is not 'thorough', it is the wrong process: the full case is prepared in initiation.

items: Tab 13.3: progress (daily log, lessons), plans (approach, PPD), risk (initial key risks), quality (expectations and requirements).
Purpose: a viable and worthwhile project? Minimum necessary; stop poorly conceived ideas.
Judge by purpose, proportion, roles, practices and tailoring.
Detail and delivery work belong to later processes and stages.

summary: You can now name the practice behind each starting up action, using the tab 13.3 extracts. You can also judge whether starting up is effective and proportionate by testing an action against the process purpose, objectives, roles and tailoring.

A.q: Carrowford City Council is starting up its half marathon project. The daily log was set up last week. Today the project manager identifies that the city's safety advisory group might not approve the event safety plan in time, and notes this uncertain event in the daily log. Which practice is being applied, and why?
options: Progress, because the daily log is set up during starting up
Risk, because starting up identifies an initial set of key risks
Issues, because the concern is noted for a later decision
Quality, because safety approval is an acceptance criterion for the event
A.why: Tab 13.3: the risk practice is applied in starting up by identifying an initial set of key risks, held in the daily log until the risk register exists.

whyNot.0: Setting up the daily log applies progress, but the log already existed; identifying the uncertain event is risk.
whyNot.2: This is an uncertain future event, so it is a risk, not an issue.
whyNot.3: Whether approval arrives in time is an uncertainty, not a quality expectation.

A.q: During starting up for the Carrowford half marathon, the project manager meets the council's senior auditor, who reviewed two earlier council events, to hear what went wrong on them. She records the points in the lessons log. Which practice is being applied?
options: Quality, because the audit findings set quality expectations
Organizing, because the auditor may later be appointed to project assurance
Plans, because past events show how the race should be run
Progress, because starting up gathers lessons from earlier work
A.why: Tab 13.3: progress is applied in starting up by setting up the daily log and gathering lessons from previous projects.

whyNot.0: Quality is applied by understanding the users' quality expectations, not by gathering lessons.
whyNot.1: No appointment is being made; the action is gathering lessons.
whyNot.2: Plans is applied by defining the approach and the PPD; recording lessons applies progress.

A.q: In starting up, Carrowford's executive and project manager decide that a specialist race company will provide course design, timing and medical cover under contract, while the council's volunteering programme recruits marshals. Which practice is being applied?
options: Plans, because this defines the project approach
Organizing, because this appoints the project team
Business case, because this selects the cheapest option
Quality, because this sets the users' expectations
A.why: Tab 13.3: plans is applied in starting up by defining the project approach (who does the work and how) and developing the PPD.

whyNot.1: Organizing appoints the PMT roles; choosing who supplies the work is the project approach.
whyNot.2: The business case justifies the project; the sourcing choice is the approach.
whyNot.3: Quality expectations describe what the event must achieve, not who delivers it.

B.q: During starting up for the Carrowford half marathon, the project manager asks the police events officer and runners' groups what standard the event must meet, for example medical response times and a certified course, so these can be captured as expectations. Which practice is being applied?
options: Risk, because medical cover failures could harm runners
Progress, because the information is noted for reporting
Quality, because it captures quality expectations
Business case, because it confirms the event's value
B.why: Tab 13.3: quality is applied in starting up by understanding the quality expectations and requirements, which go into the PPD.

whyNot.0: No uncertain event is being identified; the action is capturing the standard the event must meet.
whyNot.1: Progress covers logs and lessons; capturing expectations is quality.
whyNot.3: Value is the business case; required standards are quality expectations.

B.q: Carrowford's executive sets out, for the board, why the event is justified: the cabinet's £300,000 cap on the council's net contribution, about £2.5 million of expected local spending and the plan to repeat the event yearly. The document is kept high-level. Which practice is being applied?
options: Business case, because this is the outline justification
Progress, because the cap is a cost tolerance to monitor each stage
Risk, because the spending forecast is uncertain
Plans, because the yearly repeat is a delivery approach
B.why: Preparing the outline business case applies the business case practice: a high-level justification in the project brief (13.4.3).

whyNot.1: Tolerances are set and tracked through progress, but this document is the justification for the project.
whyNot.2: Forecasts carry uncertainty, but setting out the justification is business case work.
whyNot.3: Repeating the event is a business intention after the project, not the project approach.

B.q: In starting up, Carrowford's executive appoints the managing director of the contracted race company as senior supplier and agrees role descriptions for the board. Which practice is being applied, and why?
options: Plans, because it decides which team will deliver each product
Progress, because it sets the board's reporting lines
Quality, because it assigns who approves the products
Organizing, because it sets up the accountability structure
B.why: Appointing the PMT and agreeing role descriptions applies organizing, whose purpose is to define and establish the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities (6.1, 13.4.4).

whyNot.0: Who delivers which product is shown through the approach and work breakdown, not board appointments.
whyNot.1: Reporting lines are agreed later as project controls; appointments are organizing.
whyNot.2: Approval responsibilities for products are quality, set in product descriptions.

C.q: Carrowford's half marathon is in starting up. A board member asks the project manager to produce a full investment appraisal with detailed costs for every stage before the board decides whether to initiate. Is this an appropriate way to carry out starting up a project, and why?
options: Yes, because the cabinet's cost cap makes detailed stage costs essential
Yes, because the executive is accountable for the business case
No, because starting up does the minimum needed to decide on initiation
No, because the business case is owned by the senior user
C.why: Starting up is a lighter process that does the minimum necessary to decide whether initiation is worthwhile; the full business case is prepared in initiating a project (13.1, 15.4.5).

whyNot.0: The cap matters, but detailed costs need the project plan, which is prepared in initiation.
whyNot.1: The executive is accountable for the business case, but that does not justify detail at this point.
whyNot.3: The executive, not the senior user, is accountable for the business case.

C.q: During starting up, Carrowford's project manager identifies that a runner collapsed at a previous race managed by the contracted race company. She records the risk of a slow medical response in the daily log, because there is no risk register yet. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice in starting up, and why?
options: Yes, because the daily log replaces the risk register on events
Yes, because initial key risks are held in the daily log for now
No, because specific risks belong in the risk management approach
No, because risks should wait until the risk register is set up
C.why: Starting up identifies an initial set of key risks; they are recorded in the daily log until the risk register is set up in initiation (tab 13.3).

whyNot.0: The daily log is a temporary home; the risk register is still set up in initiation.
whyNot.2: The risk management approach holds procedures and scales, not specific risks.
whyNot.3: Waiting would lose early warning; starting up is expected to identify key risks.

C.q: Carrowford's cabinet member for leisure announces in the media that the half marathon is going ahead and asks the project manager to start booking barriers and the finish arch. The project is still in starting up and the board has not authorized initiation. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the race date is fixed and the road closures are already booked
Yes, because a cabinet member can give direction to the project
No, because starting up must first show the project is worthwhile
No, because bookings need a work package from a team manager
C.why: Starting up answers whether there is a viable and worthwhile project; the decision to start must be explicit, and delivery work comes after initiation and authorization (13.1, 2.4).

whyNot.0: A fixed date adds pressure but does not replace the explicit decision to initiate.
whyNot.1: Direction comes from the project board in directing a project, not from a cabinet member.
whyNot.3: Work packages are authorized by the PM in controlling a stage; the real problem is that nothing is authorized yet.

reteach.title: Practice spotting in starting up
reteach.question: Can you link each starting up action to its practice and say when it goes too far?

blocks.body: Logs and lessons: progress. Approach and project product description: plans. A first list of key risks: risk. What the users expect in terms of quality: quality. Then test the action: does it help decide whether initiation is worthwhile, at the least effort?

blocks.text: An option praising 'thoroughness' in starting up (detailed costs, designs, bookings) is usually wrong: the process does the minimum necessary.

explain.body: Progress is applied by setting up the daily log and gathering lessons. Risk is applied by identifying an initial set of key risks, which are noted in the daily log until the risk register is set up in initiation.

test.q: In Carrowford's starting up, the project manager creates the daily log so that she has somewhere to note informal actions and early concerns. Which practice does setting up the daily log apply?
options: Risk
Issues
Quality
Progress
test.why: Tab 13.3: progress is applied in starting up by setting up the daily log and gathering lessons.

whyNot.0: Risk is applied by identifying the initial key risks, not by creating the log.
whyNot.1: The issue register and issue management approach come in initiation.
whyNot.2: Quality is applied by understanding quality expectations and requirements.

explain.body: Plans is applied by defining the project approach and developing the project product description. Quality is applied by understanding what the users expect and require, which feeds the PPD.

test.q: Carrowford's project manager develops the project product description for the event weekend, listing the main products: the certified course, the safety plan and the riverside festival. Which practice is applied by developing the PPD in starting up?
options: Progress
Plans
Organizing
Issues
test.why: Tab 13.3: plans is applied in starting up by defining the project approach and developing the project product description.

whyNot.0: Progress covers the daily log and lessons in starting up.
whyNot.2: Organizing covers the appointments and role descriptions.
whyNot.3: The issues practice is set up in initiation with the issue management approach and register.

explain.body: The outline business case applies the business case practice: a high-level justification held in the brief. The appointments and role descriptions apply organizing: who is accountable and responsible for what.

rows.label: Activity
values: Appoint the executive, PM and PMT

test.q: For the Carrowford half marathon, the executive's role description is written to show that he owns the business case and secures the council's funding. Which practice does writing the board's role descriptions apply?
options: Business case
Plans
Organizing
Progress
test.why: Role descriptions are organizing products, created when the project management team is appointed (ch 6, 13.4.4).

whyNot.0: The content concerns the business case, but writing role descriptions is organizing.
whyNot.1: Plans covers the approach and PPD in starting up.

explain.body: An effective starting up gives the board enough to decide whether initiation is worthwhile and stops poor ideas early. It fails if it is too thin (no lessons, no PPD) or too heavy (full business case, detailed design or bookings before authority).

test.q: Carrowford's executive tells the project manager not to bother with lessons because the council has run many small markets and concerts, although nothing as large as a half marathon. How effective would starting up be if lessons were skipped?
options: Poorly, because experience from similar events may stop repeat mistakes
Well, because the events team already has relevant experience
Well, because lessons can be gathered at the end of the project
Poorly, because the business layer requires a lessons report before initiation
test.why: Assess previous lessons consults people with experience of similar projects so the project does not repeat mistakes; small markets are not similar enough to make lessons unnecessary (13.4.2, 2.2).

whyNot.1: The team has not run anything of this scale, so their experience is not a substitute for lessons.
whyNot.2: Lessons are sought at the start and throughout, not left to the end.
whyNot.3: No lessons report is required from the business layer before starting up.
